front: What is whole practice and when is it used?
back: Practising the skill in its entirety; used when the skill is fast, closed, discrete, simple, self-paced and highly organised.

front: What are the advantages of whole practice?
back: -Develops kinaesthesis. -Maintains the links between sub-routines.

front: What are the disadvantages of whole practice?
back: -Can involve too much information. -May be beyond the capabilities of the performer. -Not suitable for beginners. -Fatigue can increase the risk of injury.

front: What is whole-part-whole practice and when is it used?
back: The skill is practised as a whole, then broken down into sub-routines, before being practised as a whole again; used when the skill is complex, fast (ballistic), difficult to break down into parts, but the performer has a specific weakness.

front: What are the advantages of whole-part-whole practice?
back: -Identifies specific weaknesses. -Allows weaknesses to be corrected. -Provides immediate feedback.

front: What are the disadvantages of whole-part-whole practice?
back: -Time consuming. -Some skills cannot be broken down into parts. -Can lead to negative transfer.

front: What is progressive-part practice and when is it used?
back: The first part of the skill is practised before progressively adding the remaining parts; used when the skill is complex, serial, externally paced and low organised.

front: What are the advantages of progressive-part practice?
back: -Maintains the links between parts. -Success at each stage provides motivation. -Reduces danger. -Reduces fatigue. -Reduces the demands of the skill. -Allows focus on weaknesses.

front: What are the disadvantages of progressive-part practice?
back: -Time consuming. -If the first part is learnt incorrectly, errors can carry through the rest of the skill. -Can lead to negative transfer.

front: What is massed practice? Give a sporting example.
back: When a skill is practised continuously without a rest interval; e.g. a badminton rally where the learner repeatedly performs drop shots.

front: When is massed practice used?
back: When the skill is discrete, simple, closed, highly organised and self-paced.

front: What are the advantages of massed practice?
back: -Develops motor programmes. -Improves fitness. -Enhances overlearning. -Good for developing habitual responses. -Time-efficient.

front: What are the disadvantages of massed practice?
back: -Limited opportunity for feedback. -Fatigue. -Can be too physically and mentally demanding.

front: What is distributed practice? Give a sporting example.
back: When rest intervals are included during the practice session; e.g. completing a shooting drill for 3 minutes before receiving coach feedback and returning to practice.

front: When is distributed practice used?
back: When the skill is continuous, complex, low organised, serial and externally paced.

front: What are the advantages of distributed practice?
back: -Rest periods can be used for mental rehearsal. -Useful for physically demanding skills. -Useful when there is an element of danger. -Allows recovery.

front: What are the disadvantages of distributed practice?
back: -Time-consuming. -Can lead to negative transfer.

front: What is varied practice? Give a sporting example.
back: When different practice methods and drills are used; e.g. a netball shooting drill where the coach changes the starting position, defenders and feeder to prepare for game situations.

front: When is varied practice used?
back: When the skill is complex, open and externally paced.

front: What are the advantages of varied practice?
back: -Develops a schema. -Increases motivation. -Improves adaptability.

front: What are the disadvantages of varied practice?
back: -Time-consuming. -Can lead to negative transfer. -Fatigue. -Can be too demanding.

front: What is mental practice? Give a sporting example.
back: When the performer rehearses the skill mentally without physically performing it; e.g. a gymnast visualising themselves completing a routine.

front: What are the two types of mental practice?
back: Internal; External.

front: What is internal mental practice?
back: The performer imagines performing the skill from their own perspective, focusing on the feel of the movement.

front: What is external mental practice?
back: The performer imagines performing the skill from an external perspective, as if watching themselves on television.

front: When is mental practice used?
back: When the skill is serial and complex; used by both novice and expert performers.

front: What are the advantages of mental practice?
back: -Improves reaction time. -Develops motor programmes. -Builds confidence. -Helps control anxiety.

front: What are the disadvantages of mental practice?
back: -Must be performed correctly. -Requires a calm environment.
